recentArticles.title: Making a Will as a Single Parent: Key Legal and Practical Considerations
recentArticles.content:
Becoming a parent is a wonderful and life-changing event, and for single parents, the responsibility can feel even greater. 

One of the most important steps you can take to protect your child’s future is to make a will. A well-drafted will ensures that your wishes are respected and that your child is cared for, both emotionally and financially, should anything happen to you. Here are the key considerations for single parents when making a will.

Appointing a Guardian

Perhaps the most crucial decision for a single parent is appointing a guardian for your child. This is the person who will take on parental responsibility if you pass away before your child turns 18.

  • Choose Carefully: Consider who shares your values, has a good relationship with your child, and is willing and able to take on the role.
  • Discuss Your Choice: Speak to your chosen guardian beforehand to ensure they are comfortable with the responsibility.
  • Name a Substitute: It is helpful to name an alternative guardian in case your first choice is unable or unwilling to act when the time comes.

The legislation in this area is the Guardianship of Infants Act 1964. Section 6 of the Act provides that, on the death of the parent of an infant, any surviving parent shall be the guardian either alone or jointly with any guardian appointed under a Will. Section 7 of this Act specifies that the guardian named under the Will (testamentary guardian) shall act alongside any surviving parent as joint guardians. Either the testamentary guardian or a surviving parent can apply to court for orders pertaining to the custody of the infant.

Financial Provision for your Child

You will want to ensure that your child is financially secure. This involves deciding how your assets will be managed and distributed.

  • Trusts for Minors: Children under 18 cannot inherit directly. You can set up a trust in your will, specifying how and when your child should receive their inheritance.
  • Appointing Trustees: Trustees manage the assets on behalf of your child until they reach the age you specify (often 18 or 21). Choose people you trust to act in your child’s best interests.
  • Specific Gifts: You may wish to leave particular items or sums of money to your child or others.

You will also need to appoint an executor(s). This is the person(s) who carry out your wishes. They can be the same people as the trustees.

Letter of Wishes

While not legally binding, a letter of wishes can accompany your will. This document can provide guidance to guardians and trustees about how you would like your child to be raised, educated, or supported. 

Reviewing your Will

Circumstances change over time. Review your will regularly, especially if there are changes in your family situation, finances, or if your chosen guardian’s circumstances change. 

It is also important to let your executor, trustees, guardian know where your original Will is stored - and perhaps retain a copy at home.

Conclusion

Making a will as a single parent can be complex, particularly when trusts and guardianship are involved. It’s advisable to speak to your solicitor to ensure your will is valid and reflects your wishes accurately.

Elaine Byrne is a solicitor with Elaine Byrne Solicitors in Athboy, County Meath

recentArticles.title: What Happens to Nursing Home Debts After a Person Passes Away
recentArticles.content:
When a person dies after spending the final months or years in a nursing home, there may be a debt to the nursing home which will be due for payment.

These outstanding debts may cause stress for spouses, children and family members of the deceased. The following is a short guide to the way nursing home debts are treated in Ireland.
If in doubt, get independent legal and financial advice.

Responsibility for Nursing Home Debt

In Ireland, nursing home debt is the responsibility of the deceased's estate and is paid after their death by their personal representative (executor or administrator).

If the deceased was in the Fair Deal Scheme, any outstanding loan facility from the HSE must be repaid from the estate (funded by the sale of the deceased’s property), usually:

  • Within 12 months of death, or
  • Within 6 months if the home was sold (prior to passing away) or transferred.

Nursing homes and the HSE can claim unpaid fees from the estate. If the estate is insolvent (has insufficient assets), these debts may go unpaid.

The Deceased's Estate is Responsible for Outstanding Debts

  • Personal Representative: The executor (if there was a will) or administrator (if there was no will – known as dying intestate) will gather all the assets of the deceased.
  • Insolvent Estate: If the estate's assets aren't enough to cover the funeral expenses, administration costs, and debts, it is considered insolvent.
  • No Obligation for Children: Children of the deceased are not typically obligated to pay nursing home debts unless they were a guarantor for the debt or the debt was in their name as well. If the estate is insufficient to cover debts, the beneficiaries typically do not have to pay them personally.

Fair Deal Scheme and Loan Repayment

  • Loan Postponement: Under the Fair Deal Scheme, the HSE pays nursing home fees, and a loan can be taken out based on assets like property, with repayment postponed until after the person's death.
  • Repayment Timeline: This loan must be repaid within 12 months of the person's death, or within 6 months if their property is sold or transferred at any point.
  • Interest: If the loan is not repaid by the due date, interest will be charged from the date of death.

Process of Paying Debts

  1. Funeral and Administration Expenses: The first priority is to pay for the funeral and the expenses of managing the estate.
  2. Preferential Debts: Next are preferential debts like taxes.
  3. Ordinary Debts: Finally, other ordinary debts, such as nursing home fees and other unsecured debts (like credit cards and loans), are paid from any remaining assets.

If There Are No Assets

  • If the deceased has no assets, the debts cannot be paid, and the creditors will likely have to write off the debt.
  • The HSE and other creditors cannot claim the debt from the family of the deceased unless they are legally responsible for it.

What You Should Do

  • Contact the Executor/Administrator: If you are a family member, you should contact the personal representative to understand the estate's financial status.
  • Contact the Nursing Home: They will have details of any outstanding debts owing or that may not have been covered by the Fair Deal if the deceased was in the scheme.
  • Contact the HSE: If you are unsure about the Fair Deal loan or the outstanding fees, contact the Health Service Executive (HSE) for clarity.
  • Contact MABS: For further information, MABS – The Money Advice and Budgeting Service.
  • Fair Deal: About the Fair Deal scheme.

recentArticles.title: Creating a Space to Remember: Introducing the Anniversary Wall on RIP.ie
recentArticles.content:
For many families, anniversaries are moments of quiet reflection. A time to pause, remember, and honour the people who have shaped our lives. Over recent months, more and more families have chosen to mark these occasions by creating an Anniversary Wall on RIP.ie, a dedicated space where photographs, memories and messages can be shared with loved ones near and far.

The Anniversary Wall offers a simple, meaningful way to keep someone’s memory alive throughout the year. Whether it’s a first anniversary or a special date that holds personal significance, this space allows families and friends to come together in remembrance, no matter where they are.

A place to gather memories

Each Anniversary Wall includes:

A photo gallery — up to five cherished images that capture moments, milestones and memories.

A message wall — a space where others can share their thoughts, stories and tributes.

Automatic sharing — your loved one’s Anniversary Wall is shared to your county’s RIP.ie Facebook page, helping friends and neighbours join in remembrance.

A full year of visibility — allowing people to visit and revisit whenever they wish.

These features come together to create a lasting tribute.

Simple to create, meaningful to share

Setting up an Anniversary Wall takes only a few moments. Families can log in to their RIP.ie account, select Family Notices, and choose Anniversary Wall to begin.

For many, it becomes a comforting place to return to — a digital space that holds photographs, words, and the presence of those who continue to be loved and remembered.

Keeping memories alive

Grief doesn’t follow a calendar, and remembrance doesn’t begin or end on a single day. The Anniversary Wall offers families a gentle way to honour their loved one, share memories with others, and keep their story present in the lives of those who cared for them.

If you feel this might be helpful for you or your family, you can learn more or begin creating an Anniversary Wall whenever the time feels right.

recentArticles.title: Keeping Watch: An Irish Reflection on the Vigil and the Transition Into Death
recentArticles.content:
Brendan Gleeson on Presence and the Gift of Being There

In an interview with Newstalk in 2024, Brendan Gleeson spoke of a friend's motivation for learning Irish; "[I]t's a dying language or whatever, but if your mother was dying, you wouldn't want her to die alone […] I feel the gift of it. And while it's there, I want to be in its presence."

I think Ireland's attitude towards the dying, our reason for keeping watch over them as they are passing, is very much the same. We understand the gift of our loved ones, and while they are there, even if they are going from us, we want to be in their presence. We want to watch over them and remind them that they are not alone.

Witnessing Death for the First Time

I was sixteen when I first watched someone transition into death.

That's what hospice sites refer to it as: a transition. Dying, as living, is not always an instance, but a process. I have witnessed the transition into death twice. It was not graceful, or beautiful. But the vigil, the watching — maybe only in retrospect — was made beautiful by its constituent parts: love, care, compassion, kindness, and respect, to name a few.

Family, Music and the Final Hours

As my grandmother lay dying, my family gathered around her bed and sang Christmas songs and hymns. She no longer remembered who we were, but she mouthed the words along with us, even when her mouth grew dry and cracked, the effort even to close her lips too much.

When my grandfather, her husband, was dying a few years later, we gathered in the care home with our Christmas dinners, and took turns keeping him company. We'd usually spend Christmas Day at my grandparents' house, anyway, so we took on a familiar routine in a strange place. We exchanged stories and told jokes and had to fight to keep our voices and laughter down, in between fits of tears.

The Strange Experience of Time During a Vigil

Time became strange. The days and nights I spent in care homes watching my grandparents transition into death felt endless. When they crossed over, and we began to make funeral arrangements, it was like I was jolted from a stupor. Time had paused and then rushed to catch up with itself, a tape that had caught, frozen, then stuttered ahead to the end of the song.

Irish Traditions of Keeping Watch

I had not considered the vigil, the watching, the witnessing, as something unusual or different to other cultures around the world. I don't remember the moment I learned that we keep a person company while they transition into death; it feels like something I have always known, always taken as a given.

A Different Cultural Lens on Death

In her podcast, "All Miracles Are Strange", American artist Lizz Hamilton recounted her family keeping vigil over her dying grandmother (episode 6, "To Witness", 2023). Listening to her reflections, I understood, for the first time, that not everyone confronted and processed the dead and dying like I did. I was hit with a new appreciation, even gratitude, for Irish traditions around death.

When I reached out to Hamilton — to offer condolences, and share a little about how commonplace it is in Ireland to watch over the dying — she described the sharp difference in the American experience:

"I don't know what the news is like in Ireland, but it is often the only place Americans ever see a dead body, and only then in moments of excruciating violence […] All the slow deaths seem relegated to hospitals and care homes, tended only by professionals. The hospice nurses who cared for my grandmother felt like shamans, coming to us with otherworldly knowledge about a process that is held in total secrecy."

The Pain and the Gift of Being Present

Watching my grandparents leave me, slowly, over the course of months and then days, was one of the most painful experiences of my life. I cannot pretend like it was all beautiful, and transcendant, and spiritual. But it would be equally untrue to say I was not grateful for those experiences.

If I could turn back the clock, I would not shy away from the vigil. I would not avert my gaze, or crawl into my bed and pretend that nothing was happening. I would not trade that last bit of time with my grandparents for anything.

The Transition for the Living

I wanted to be with them while they transitioned, changed. And I, the witness, underwent a change of my own. I began my own transition from a life with them, to a life without them.

Even with all of the pain, the sleepless nights, the strange liminality, even though my being there could not have stopped or changed the outcome, my presence still mattered. My love still mattered.

The Miracle of Looking

Hamilton called "the looking" a miracle, and I couldn't help but agree. It is a miracle, to be here with you, the dying, now. I feel the gift of it, and while you are here, I want to be in your presence.

recentArticles.title: A Mother’s Grief, A Community’s Strength: Eileen Loughlin Shares Annabel’s Story on Parting Words
recentArticles.content:
In the latest episode of Parting Words, primary school teacher and content creator Eileen Loughlin speaks with remarkable honesty about the loss of her three‑and‑a‑half‑year‑old daughter, Annabel, who died in 2018 following a tragic accident in the family home. It is a conversation filled with courage, tenderness and the quiet strength that so often defines Irish families in the face of unthinkable loss.

Eileen describes the morning of the accident as completely ordinary: mid‑term break, children playing, plans to go to the cinema. Within hours, Annabel had been airlifted to Temple Street, where a team of doctors fought to save her. Eileen recalls lying beside her daughter, singing to her and holding her until she died. 

“I really felt like her spirit left her body… Annabel is gone. But her spirit is still here with us.

What followed were days that no parent imagines navigating. Eileen and her husband Enda brought Annabel home and laid her in her own bed. Family, neighbours and friends kept vigil around the clock. Food arrived at the door. People travelled from England, Australia and Taiwan to stand with them. “It was the real Irish wake,” Eileen says. “The community rallied. Things happened that we will never even know about.”

Throughout the episode, Eileen speaks openly about parenting through grief — supporting her sons, welcoming her youngest daughter Isla, and keeping Annabel present in their home in small, everyday ways. Her room remains open. Her lamp is switched on each morning. Isla, who never met her sister, still says “Bye Annabel” as she leaves the room.

Eileen also reflects on the support that helped her family survive those early months: the bereavement team at Temple Street, the grounding routine of school and sport.

This episode of Parting Words is a testament to the power of community, the rituals that hold us, and the enduring bond between a mother and her child. It is tender, brave and full of heart — a reminder that even in the darkest moments, love does not end.

About the Sponsor: An Post Insurance

Parting Words is proudly sponsored by An Post Insurance. The partnership reflects the company’s commitment to supporting people as they prepare thoughtfully and compassionately for life’s most difficult moments. The podcast aligns naturally with An Post Insurance’s funeral insurance product, which helps individuals plan ahead and ease the financial burden on loved ones during times of loss.

One Direct (Ireland) Limited, trading as An Post Insurance, is regulated by the Central Bank of Ireland. It is a wholly owned subsidiary of An Post and is a tied agent of New Ireland Assurance Company plc for life assurance business. Funeral Insurance policies are underwritten and provided by New Ireland Assurance Company plc.

recentArticles.title: When a Friend Dies Suddenly: Daragh Fleming on the Reality of Suicide Grief
recentArticles.content:
Suicide grief is unlike any other form of loss. 

It arrives without warning, without preparation, and without the gentle anticipations that sometimes accompany illness or old age. It is a grief filled with shock, confusion, guilt, unanswered questions and a silence that can swallow families whole.

In Episode Four of Parting Words, writer and poet Daragh Fleming sits with Muireann O’Connell to speak openly about this kind of grief, the kind that reshapes a life in an instant.

Daragh was 17 when his best friend, Erbie Underwood, died after attempting to take his own life. The two had grown up together through basketball, forming the kind of friendship that becomes a defining part of who you are. When Erbie died, Daragh’s world did not just change; it collapsed.

The Shock That Never Leaves

Daragh describes the moment he learned the truth. He arrived at the hospital with friends, expecting to visit Erbie as he recovered, and was instead led into a quiet room where Erbie’s mother told them he was gone. It is a moment that many families affected by suicide will recognise: the suddenness, the disbelief, the sense that the world has tilted off its axis.

Suicide grief often begins with shock, but it rarely ends there.

The Questions That Have No Answers

One of the most painful aspects of suicide loss is the search for meaning in something that cannot be explained. Daragh speaks about the guilt he carried for years, including the small, ordinary moment when he turned down a lunch invitation from Erbie on the day of the attempt he would not survive.

It is a detail that will resonate deeply with anyone who has lost someone to suicide. The mind clings to tiny moments, replaying them endlessly, as if the right combination of memories might unlock an answer. But suicide grief rarely offers answers. It offers only love, longing and the slow work of acceptance.

The Silence Around Suicide, Especially for Young Men

Daragh also speaks about how invisible Erbie’s struggle was. “He was really good at acting,” he says. “I had no idea he was struggling.”

This silence is something many families know too well. Young men, in particular, are often taught to hide their pain, to stay composed, to keep going. That silence can be dangerous. And for those left behind, it can deepen the grief, adding layers of confusion and self-blame.

By speaking openly about this silence, Daragh helps dismantle the stigma that still surrounds suicide loss.

When Grief Becomes Numbness

For Daragh, grief did not look like tears or sadness. It became four years of emotional numbness, a complete absence of feeling that he did not yet understand as depression.

“I was not sad. I was not happy. I was not anything,” he says.

This, too, is part of suicide grief. It can flatten a person, hollow them out, leave them moving through life without connection or colour. It is a grief that affects the body as much as the mind.

Finding a Way Back Through Words

Daragh eventually found his way back to emotion through writing. Journaling became a lifeline, and poetry became the tool that helped him relearn how to feel. Today, his poems often go viral for their honesty and vulnerability, resonating with people who recognise their own unspoken feelings in his words.

His voice matters because he names what so many people experience but struggle to articulate.

Why This Episode Matters

Suicide grief is often carried quietly. Families may feel isolated, unsure how to talk about what happened, or afraid of saying the wrong thing. But silence does not protect us. It only deepens the pain.

This episode of Parting Words is an invitation to break that silence.

It reminds us that talking about suicide does not cause harm. Not talking about it does.

It reminds us that guilt is common, but it is not a burden anyone should carry alone. It reminds us that numbness is not failure; it is a response to trauma. And it reminds us that love does not end when a life ends.

Daragh’s story is not just about loss. It is about the courage it takes to speak, to feel again, and to honour someone’s memory by telling the truth.

You can watch Episode Four on YouTube or listen on all major podcast platforms.

If you or someone you love has been affected by suicide, support is available. You can reach out to the Samaritans for confidential emotional support at any time, or connect with HUGG, a peer support organisation for people bereaved by suicide. You do not have to carry this alone, and speaking to someone who understands can make a real difference.

Alerts.title: My Email Alerts
Alerts.createAlertDescription: Get an email each time a new death notice is published which matches your selected “surname” “town” “county” or “church”.
Alerts.tips: Tips for alerts by Surname / County / Town
Alerts.alertsDescription: To receive alerts for funerals at specific churches:
Alerts.selectChurch: Select church county from the dropdown list
Alerts.selectDenomination: Select church denomination from the dropdown list
Alerts.selectActualChurch: Select actual church for from the dropdown list
Alerts.countyTipOne: Get alerts for all deaths in a county - select that county
Alerts.countyTipTwo: A specific town(s) - set each town as a separate alert. If a town straddles two counties, set an alert for that town in each county
Alerts.countyTipThree: A specific person - set "surname" & "county" of the person. Where a surname may be spelled a number of ways, set an alert for each variation
Alerts.countyTipFour: Sometimes "town" is not included in the notice, so you may prefer to keep your search at the "county" level.
Alerts.repeatChurch: Repeat for each church you want alerts for
Alerts.minOneField: Min. one field should be filled!
Alerts.sureSuspendAlert: Are you sure you want to temporarily suspend this alert?
Alerts.sureRestartAlert: Are you sure you want to restart this alert?
Alerts.alertyDeleteAsk: Are you sure you want to delete this alert?
Alerts.error: There was an error! Please try again!
